title: Verbs that slip into the middle
goal: Use *-um-* and *ma-* verbs, see why the infix goes inside the word, and know how they differ from *mag-*.
bekal: inserting *-um-* after the root's first consonant
building *-um-* and *ma-* aspects without mixing them up with *mag-*
choosing *mag-* or *-um-* for roots that take both

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Kumain ka na ba?
dialogs.intro: Almost noon. Ana checks on Budi, who has just woken up after staying up late.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Not yet. I just woke up.

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.id: What time did you go to bed last night?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Natulog ako ng alas-dos. Nag-aral kasi ako.
lines.id: I slept at two. I was studying, see.
lines.literal: slept I at two-o'clock. studied because I.

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.text: Naku! Kumain ka muna, tapos matulog ka ulit.
lines.id: Oh dear! Eat first, then go back to sleep.
lines.literal: oh-dear! eat you first, then sleep you again.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Uminom muna ako ng kape. May kape pa ba?
lines.id: I'll have some coffee first. Is there any coffee left?
lines.literal: drink first I of coffee. there's coffee still Q?

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.text: Meron pa. Bumili ako kanina sa tindahan.
lines.id: There's still some. I bought some at the shop earlier.
lines.literal: there's still. bought I earlier at shop.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Salamat, Ate! Saan ka pupunta mamaya?
lines.id: Thanks, Sis! Where are you going later?
lines.literal: thanks, Big-Sis! where you will-go later?

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.text: Pupunta ako sa palengke. Sasama ka ba?
lines.id: I'm going to the market. Want to come?
lines.literal: will-go I to market. will-come-along you Q?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Sasama ako! Maliligo lang ako, sandali.
lines.id: I'm coming! Just let me shower, one moment.
lines.literal: will-come-along I! will-bathe just I, moment.

notes: **-um- is an infix, not a prefix.** It goes **inside** the root, right after the first consonant: *kain* → *k-um-ain* → *kumain*. Roots that start with a vowel take it at the front: *inom* → *uminom*, *alis* → *umalis*. English has nothing like this outside jokes like "abso-bloody-lutely"; Malay and Indonesian keep fossil traces of the same infix.

**The "done" form and the basic -um- form are identical.** *Kumain* means both "eat" (basic form) and "ate". Only the context tells them apart: after *gusto*, *huwag* or *dapat*, it hasn't happened yet. This is economy, not confusion — once you're used to it, it's one less form to learn.
**The "coming" form of -um- drops the infix.** *Kakain* (will eat), not *kukumain*. All that remains is the repeated first syllable of the root. This is the form beginners get wrong most often.

**Ma- marks a state that happens to the doer.** *Matulog* (sleep), *magutom* (get hungry), *maligo* (bathe), *mapagod* (get tired). The doer isn't fully acting — they're experiencing. The aspects follow the pattern you know: *ma-* becomes *na-* once started.

**Kagigising ko lang** uses a special form meaning "just did": the prefix *ka-* + repetition + root. Its cousins: *kararating lang* (just arrived), *kakakain lang* (just ate). Very common and worth learning whole.
**Kasi means "because, see"** and usually goes in the middle or at the end, not at the front like English "because": *Nag-aral kasi ako.* The more formal word is *dahil*.

**Natulog ako ng alas-dos** uses *ng* to mark time. This is a use of *ng* you haven't seen yet: besides possession and objects, it also marks time and manner. *Ng alas-dos* (at two), *ng mabilis* (quickly).

**Muna means "first"** in the sense of sequence: *Kumain ka muna* (eat first), *Sandali muna* (hold on a moment). One of the most useful particles, and easy, because it works just like English "first" at the end of a request.
**Sasama ka ba?** comes from the root *sama* (go along, together). It also gives *kasama* (companion) and *magkasama* (together) — a word family you'll use a lot.

grammars.title: The three stages of -um- verbs
body: Look at the second and third columns: they're identical. Not a typo — that's how *-um-* verbs really work.
after: Note *dumarating* — the root is *dating*, but *d* becomes *r* when squeezed between two vowels. The sound rule from the pronunciation pages at work.
The "coming" form never contains *-um-*: *kakain*, *iinom*, *pupunta*, *aalis*. If you catch yourself saying *kukumain*, stop and try again.
Roots starting with a vowel repeat that vowel: *inom* → *iinom*, *alis* → *aalis*, *upo* → *uupo*. Odd in writing, natural in speech.

grammars.title: Ma- verbs — experienced, not done
body: A small group, but full of words you'll use every day.
after: For bodily states, the "ongoing" form is the most common: *Nagugutom ako* (I'm hungry), *Napapagod ako* (I'm tired), *Nauuhaw ako* (I'm thirsty).
Note that *natulog* means "slept" — a finished action — while "is sleeping" is *natutulog*. Pick the wrong one and you'll tell a midnight caller "I slept" instead of "I was sleeping".
*Matuto* differs from *mag-aral*: the first means to master something, the second to study it. *Nag-aral ako ng Tagalog* (I studied), *Natuto akong mag-Tagalog* (I learned to speak it).

blocks.text: Some roots take both, and the meaning shifts. No rule holds one hundred percent, but the tendency is clear enough to use.
If you're really unsure, pick the form you hear most. Living languages don't wait for rules: *kumain*, *uminom*, *pumunta*, *umalis*, *matulog* are used in that form and almost never in another.

blocks.title: The sentence you'll hear most
items: *Kumain ka na ba?* — "Have you eaten?" It's a greeting, not a real question; in the Philippines it's the equivalent of "how are you?" — and is often followed by a very real offer of food.
Safe answers: *Kumain na po ako, salamat.* or *Hindi pa po.* If you give the second one, be ready to actually be told to eat.

blocks.text: These fifteen verbs plus the fifteen *mag-* verbs from the last unit are enough to describe a whole day — which is exactly what you'll do in unit 20.
